svg.title: Who needs post-operative radiotherapy: a clinic map of surgery by nodes
svg.desc: Schematic clinic map of who needs post-operative radiotherapy, built on two variables: the type of surgery (breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy) and the axillary nodes (negative, positive, and how many). The cells carry three labels that are not interchangeable: recommended, a decision to discuss, and not a routine indication. Breast-conserving surgery with negative nodes is labelled recommended — whole breast irradiation is part of the package, not an add-on: the EBCTCG meta-analysis (17 trials, 7,287 pN0 women) found any first recurrence at 10 years falling from 31.0% to 15.6% and breast cancer death at 15 years from 20.5% to 17.2%; the landmark NSABP B-06 trial at 20 years found cumulative ipsilateral breast recurrence of 39.2% after lumpectomy alone against 14.3% with irradiation; older patients with small, hormone-receptor-positive tumours have omission to discuss, with the conditions and trade-offs set out in a separate article. Breast-conserving surgery with positive nodes is also labelled recommended: the same meta-analysis (1,050 pN+ women, a small group with wide confidence intervals) found recurrence at 10 years falling from 63.7% to 42.5% and breast cancer death at 15 years from 51.3% to 42.8%; whether the regional nodes are treated as well is a separate decision. Mastectomy with negative nodes, meaning no positive nodes after axillary clearance, is labelled not a routine indication: among 700 women in the EBCTCG meta-analysis, irradiation lowered neither recurrence nor breast cancer death, with rate ratios of 1.06 and 1.18, neither significant. Mastectomy with positive nodes splits into two cells. One to three positive nodes is labelled a decision to discuss: the older meta-analysis of 1,314 women found chest wall plus regional nodal irradiation bringing the breast cancer mortality rate ratio to 0.80 (95% confidence interval 0.67 to 0.95), but SUPREMO, reported in 2025, repeated the question on modern systemic therapy in 1,607 women with median follow-up of 9.6 years and found 10-year overall survival of 81.4% against 81.9% (hazard ratio 1.04, p value 0.80, no difference) with chest wall recurrence of 1.1% against 2.5% (hazard ratio 0.45, a difference); the interventions differ too, the older trials treating chest wall plus regional nodes and SUPREMO the chest wall only — so this cell is neither an automatic yes nor an automatic no, but a decision taken with node count, tumour size, grade and lymphovascular invasion all on the table. Only four or more positive nodes is labelled recommended: the older meta-analysis of 1,772 women found an overall recurrence rate ratio of 0.79 and a breast cancer mortality rate ratio of 0.87, and no randomised trial repeating the question on modern drugs has challenged this cell. The figure closes with two reminders: both EBCTCG meta-analyses recruited in the 1960s to 1980s, so absolute figures for patients treated today are generally lower than the table and the proportional effect is the more reliable part, a label that cannot be dropped; and this is a clinic map rather than a verdict, with the final placing settled by the treating team on the full pathology, imaging and systemic therapy plan, since radiotherapy changes the odds and is not an insurance policy.

g.text: WHO NEEDS POST-OPERATIVE RADIOTHERAPY
Who needs post-operative
radiotherapy: a clinic map of
surgery by nodes
Two variables decide the cell: breast-conserving surgery or
mastectomy, and whether the axillary nodes are involved and in
what number.
The cells carry three different labels — recommended, a decision
to be discussed, and not a routine indication. They are not
interchangeable.
Breast-conserving surgery (PM) ／ Node negative
Recommended
Whole breast irradiation is part of the package, not
an add-on
EBCTCG meta-analysis (17 trials, 7,287 pN0 women): any first
recurrence at 10 years fell from 31.0% to 15.6%, and breast
cancer death at 15 years from 20.5% to 17.2%.
The landmark NSABP B-06 trial at 20 years: cumulative
ipsilateral breast recurrence 39.2% after lumpectomy alone, and
14.3% with irradiation.
Older patients with small, hormone-receptor-positive tumours
have omission to discuss; the conditions and the trade-offs
have an article of their own.
Mastectomy (including modified radical, MRM) ／ Node negative
Not a routine indication
No positive nodes after axillary clearance
EBCTCG meta-analysis (700 women): irradiation lowered neither
recurrence nor breast cancer death — rate ratios 1.06 and 1.18,
neither significant.
So node-negative disease after mastectomy is not a routine
indication.
Breast-conserving surgery (PM) ／ Node positive
Recommended
Node-positive breast-conserving surgery
The same meta-analysis (1,050 pN+ women, a small group with
wide confidence intervals): recurrence at 10 years fell from
63.7% to 42.5%, and breast cancer death at 15 years from 51.3%
Whether the regional nodes are treated as well is a separate
decision.
The proportional reduction is much the same across groups, but
the higher your own baseline risk, the larger the absolute
number irradiation takes off — so the same table reads
differently for each person.
Mastectomy (including modified radical, MRM) ／ Node positive
A decision to discuss
1 to 3 positive nodes
The older meta-analysis (1,314 women): chest wall plus regional
nodal irradiation brought the breast cancer mortality rate
ratio to 0.80 (95% confidence interval 0.67 to 0.95).
SUPREMO, reported in 2025, repeated the question on modern
systemic therapy (1,607 women, median follow-up 9.6 years):
10-year overall survival 81.4% against 81.9% (hazard ratio
1.04, p=0.80, no difference); chest wall recurrence 1.1%
against 2.5% (hazard ratio 0.45, a difference).
The interventions differ too: the older trials treated chest
wall plus regional nodes, SUPREMO the chest wall only. So this
cell is neither an automatic yes nor an automatic no — it is a
decision taken with node count, tumour size, grade and
lymphovascular invasion all on the table.
Mastectomy (including modified radical, MRM) ／ Node positive
Recommended
4 or more positive nodes
The older meta-analysis (1,772 women): overall recurrence rate
ratio 0.79 and breast cancer mortality rate ratio 0.87.
And no randomised trial repeating the question on modern drugs
has challenged this cell.
How to read these figures
Both EBCTCG meta-analyses recruited in the 1960s to 1980s:
absolute figures for patients treated today are generally lower
than the table, and the proportional effect is the more
reliable part — that label cannot be dropped.
This is a clinic map, not a verdict: where you land is settled
by your own team on the full pathology, imaging and systemic
therapy plan. Radiotherapy changes the odds; it is not an
insurance policy.
Schematic, redrawn from EBCTCG 2011, EBCTCG 2014, Kunkler 2025 (SUPREMO) and
Fisher 2002 (NSABP B-06)
Eras, cohorts and treated volumes differ between studies; figures are not
directly comparable across cells
